newsitem.title: USA: Mexico has not supported peso in 1996 - Buira.
newsitem.headline: Mexico has not supported peso in 1996 - Buira.

text.p: Bank of Mexico Deputy Governor Ariel Buira said on Friday that the central bank has not intervened this year to support the peso, and added that the value of the currency is determined by the market.
"Not once in 1996 has the central bank dispersed one single dollar to support the peso," Buira said.

Buira said that the central bank believed the peso's value should be determined by market forces, and would only intervene to protect its level in "extreme conditions to preserve orderly market conditions."
"Supply and demand will determine the rate of the peso," Buira said. "We do not have an exchange rate objective. The exchange rate is freely floating."

Buira, who was a panelist at the Emerging Markets roundtable here, made the comments in response to fellow panelist Frank Fernandez, senior portfolio manager at Global Emerging Market Advisors, who suggested the Bank of Mexico had managed a 18 percent real appreciation of the peso this year.
"The assertion is that we have managed the exchange rate," Buira said. "This is flatly false."
Market rumors that Mexico has influenced the peso's value have persisted. But the deputy governor said that the peso's strength was linked to Mexico's surge in exports.
"Any country that is a successful exporter will have an appreciation in its exchange rate," Buira said.
Buira noted that Mexico had held an auction in August to accumulate dollar reserves, but this process had no effect on the value of the currency.
"If the central bank intervened to support the peso, this would come out in the weekly reserve figures," Buira said.
